findings.claim: On days they worked at home, employed people spent an average of 5.10 hours working at home. Even on a day the work laptop IS used at home, it is work-active ~5 hours, leaving ~19 of 24 idle.
findings.number: 5.10 hours/day worked at home
findings.source: BLS American Time Use Survey, Table 6 (2025 annual averages), fetched via web.archive.org mirror of bls.gov/news.release/atus.t06.htm

findings.claim: Of employed people who worked on an average day, 34.5% did some or all of their work at home; 69.8% worked at their workplace. ATUS counts ANY work at home, not a full day.
findings.number: 34.5% any work at home; 69.8% at workplace (of those who worked)
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 annual averages (archive.org mirror)

findings.claim: Full-time workers at home averaged 5.35 h of work at home vs 8.21 h at the workplace. Work done at home is ~2.9 h/day shorter: the at-home machine is lower duty cycle even on days it is used.
findings.number: 5.35 h at home vs 8.21 h at workplace (full-time)
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 annual averages (archive.org mirror)

findings.claim: Degree-holders, the population most likely to be issued a company laptop, worked at home on 51.4% of days worked, averaging 5.18 hours of at-home work. High incidence, still only ~5 hours.
findings.number: 51.4% incidence; 5.18 h/day at home (bachelor's degree and higher)
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 annual averages (archive.org mirror)

findings.claim: DERIVED: expected at-home work hours per employed person per day worked = 0.345 x 5.10. Averaged over all workers, a work machine at home is in active work use under two hours per workday.
findings.number: ~1.76 hours/worker/day worked
findings.source: Derived from BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 (34.5% x 5.10 h)
findings.caveat: Arithmetic derivation by me, not a published BLS figure; mixes zero-at-home days into the mean.

findings.claim: Pre-pandemic: in 2018 only 23.7% worked at home on days worked, averaging 2.94 h at home vs 7.94 at workplace. The classic laptop-carried-home regime: ~0.70 h/worker/day expected.
findings.number: 2.94 h/day at home; 23.7% incidence (2018); derived 0.70 h/worker/day
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, 2018 annual averages, via web.archive.org 2019 snapshot of bls.gov/news.release/atus.t06.htm

findings.claim: At-home work duration jumped then plateaued: 2.94 h (2018) to 5.41 h (2022) to ~5.12 h to 5.10 h (2025); incidence 23.7% to 33.8% to 34.6% to 34.5%. Tier B is flat, not still growing.
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, successive annual averages, four web.archive.org snapshots of bls.gov/news.release/atus.t06.htm
findings.caveat: The intermediate 5.12 h / 34.6% snapshot's table header was truncated in extraction; it is the 2023 or 2024 annual average. 2018/2022/2025 are unambiguous.

findings.claim: Full-day (6+ h) home work is rarer than any-work-at-home: 28% of paid full days were WFH days (Sept 2024, SWAA) vs 34.5% doing some work at home (ATUS). The gap is the barely-opened-laptop population.
findings.number: 28% of paid full days WFH (Sept 2024)
findings.source: Barrero, Bloom, Buckman & Davis, SWAA January 2025 Updates deck, slide 5 (wfhresearch.com PDF, fetched directly)

findings.claim: Tier A remains the bulk: mid-2024, 61% of US full-time employees worked all days on business premises, 27% hybrid, 12% fully remote. Only ~39% generate any Tier-B machine-hours in a given week.
findings.number: 61% fully on-site / 27% hybrid / 12% fully remote
findings.source: Barrero, Bloom, Buckman & Davis, SWAA January 2025 Updates deck, slide 11 (wfhresearch.com PDF, fetched directly)

findings.claim: Employer plans for work-from-home trend near 2.3 days/week for employees able to WFH: for that subset roughly 2-3 of 5 workdays place the machine at a residence rather than on premises.
findings.number: ~2.3 days/week planned WFH (WFH-able employees)
findings.source: Barrero, Bloom, Buckman & Davis, SWAA January 2025 Updates deck, slide 7 (wfhresearch.com PDF, fetched directly)

findings.claim: EU comparison (incidence only, no duration): in 2024, 8.9% of employed persons 15-64 usually worked from home, 13.7% sometimes, 77.4% never. Tier B is proportionally much smaller in the EU.
findings.number: 8.9% usually / 13.7% sometimes / 77.4% never (EU27, 2024)
findings.source: Eurostat dataset lfsa_ehomp, fetched via Eurostat dissemination API (ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/lfsa_ehomp)

findings.claim: DERIVED Tier-B idle budget: ~18.9 h idle on a day the laptop is home and used (79% of the calendar day), ~10.9 h against a 16 h waking day, ~24 h on a day it goes home unopened.
findings.number: ~18.9 h idle on a used day; ~24 h on an unused day
findings.source: Derived from BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 (5.10 h at home)
findings.caveat: Arithmetic derivation, not published. Excludes personal (non-work) use of the same machine, which ATUS does not measure and which would shrink the harvestable window.

findings.claim: Tier A cross-check: workplace workers averaged 7.87 h of work there (8.21 full-time), so an on-premises machine is work-active ~8 of 24 h, leaving ~16 h/day plus weekends - consistent with the LBNL empty-dock finding.
findings.number: 7.87 h/day at workplace (8.21 full-time) -> ~16 h/day idle
findings.source: BLS ATUS Table 6, 2025 annual averages (archive.org mirror)

time-use-duration.notes: No WebSearch used. bls.gov reached via web.archive.org mirrors of news.release/atus.t06.htm at four timestamps, plus atus.nr0.htm and atus.t04.htm. SWAA deck pulled directly from wfhresearch.com and converted with pdftotext. Eurostat via its open dissemination API (frequenc index SMT=0, USU=1, NVR=2 read from the API's own category index; values 13.7/8.9/77.4). OpenAlex searches for peer-reviewed after-hours work DURATION studies returned nothing usable; the one on-topic hit (doi 10.1080/1359432x.2023.2225773) measures intentions and frequency, not machine-hours, so it is excluded. No vendor telemetry fetched, so none reported. Headline: Tier B machine-hours are real but low duty cycle and flat since 2022 - ~5.1 h of at-home work on days it happens, ~1.8 h averaged over all workdays, vs a pre-pandemic 2.9 h / 0.7 h baseline. The resource relocates rather than disappears; what changes is who pays power and which uplink it sits behind. Caveat on all ATUS at-home figures: BLS footnote 2 says they include any work at home and are not restricted to people whose usual workplace is home.

findings.claim: Company laptops at home are used for work only ~5.1 hours on a day work is done at home — the duration measure, not incidence
findings.number: 5.10 avg hours of work at home (employed 15+); 5.35 h full-time; 5.18 h bachelor's degree and higher
findings.source: BLS American Time Use Survey 2025 annual averages, Table 6 (fetched via web.archive.org snapshot 20260724 of bls.gov/news.release/atus.t06.htm; last modified 2026-06-25)
findings.caveat: ATUS 'work at home' covers any work done at home, not necessarily on an employer-issued laptop; it is person-time, not device-on time.

findings.claim: Work-at-home is a minority of workdays even among those who work: only about a third of people who worked on an average day did any of it at home
findings.number: 34.5% of those who worked; 51.4% among bachelor's-and-higher; 37.837M worked at home on an average day of 167.443M employed (22.6%)
findings.source: BLS ATUS 2025 annual averages, Table 6 (archived bls.gov/news.release/atus.t06.htm)

findings.claim: DERIVED: a company laptop that goes home is idle the overwhelming majority of wall-clock time — the resource relocates rather than disappears, and Tier B's harvestable window is large
findings.number: 5.10 h of 24 h = 78.8% idle on a work-at-home day; weighted by 34.5% incidence, ~1.76 h/day expected use = ~92.7% of hours idle
findings.source: Derived by this analysis from BLS ATUS 2025 Table 6 (5.10 h, 34.5%)
findings.caveat: Derived arithmetic, not a published BLS statistic. Assumes laptop use tracks the person's at-home work hours and ignores sleep/lid-closed states, which reduce harvestable hours further.

findings.claim: Cloud MDM reaches off-network devices: Intune runs entirely in the cloud, and compliance decisions are explicitly decoupled from network location
findings.number: "runs entirely in the cloud, with no on-premises infrastructure required"; decisions based on device posture "not on whether the device is on the corporate network"
findings.source: Microsoft Learn, 'What is Microsoft Intune?', learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/intune-service/fundamentals/what-is-intune (ms.date 2026-05-06)

findings.claim: Intune management traffic is ordinary outbound HTTPS to public endpoints — no VPN, gateway, or corporate LAN in the path
findings.number: "As a cloud-only service, Intune doesn't require an on-premises infrastructure such as servers or gateways"; all endpoints public FQDNs on TCP 80/443
findings.source: Microsoft Learn, 'Network endpoints for Microsoft Intune', learn.microsoft.com/en-us/mem/intune/fundamentals/intune-endpoints (updated 2026-07-01)

findings.claim: Apple MDM push works over any consumer internet connection, not a corporate network
findings.number: APNs needs "a persistent connection to Apple's servers over Ethernet, cellular data (if capable), or Wi-Fi"; TCP 5223, plus 443 or 2197; Apple 17.0.0.0/8
findings.source: Apple Support article 102266, 'If your Apple devices aren't getting Apple push notifications' (published 2023-08-22)

findings.claim: Apple Declarative Device Management strengthens the off-network case: devices apply and enforce policy autonomously, without server polling or continuous connectivity
findings.number: device "asynchronously appl[ies] settings and report[s] status back... without constant polling"; stays in desired state "even without internet connectivity"
findings.source: Apple Platform Deployment guide, 'Intro to declarative device management' (support.apple.com/guide/deployment/depb1bab77f8)

findings.claim: Harvesting on an employee's meter costs ~31% more per kWh than harvesting on the business's meter
findings.number: US avg retail price YTD Jan-May 2026: residential 18.11 vs commercial 13.79 c/kWh = 1.31x; May 2026 alone 18.44 vs 13.54 = 1.36x
findings.source: EIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.3 (eia.gov/electricity/monthly), data through May 2026
findings.caveat: EIA notes 2025 and 2026 values are preliminary estimates based on a cutoff model sample.

findings.claim: DERIVED: the energy-to-harvest figure re-priced at residential rates stays negligible against revenue
findings.number: ~$0.003/hr commercial scales to ~$0.0039-0.0041/hr residential (x1.31-1.36) vs $0.05-0.20/hr spot-like revenue
findings.source: Derived from the project's existing ~$0.003/hr energy figure and EIA EPM Table 5.3 residential/commercial ratio
findings.caveat: Derived. Excludes residential time-of-use premia, which can materially raise evening/overnight marginal rates in CA and NY.

findings.claim: US law can force the employer to pay: California Labor Code 2802 is a mandatory indemnity for necessary expenditures incurred in obeying the employer
findings.number: "shall indemnify his or her employee for all necessary expenditures or losses incurred by the employee in direct consequence of the discharge of his or her duties"
findings.source: California Labor Code 2802(a), leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (lawCode=LAB, sectionNum=2802)

findings.claim: Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service (2014) extended 2802 to require reasonable reimbursement of home utilities and phone used for work even absent marginal cost — the leading home-expense authority
findings.number: Cochran v. Schwan's Home Serv., Inc., 228 Cal. App. 4th 1137 (2014)
findings.source: Cited from model knowledge; opinion not fetchable under the no-WebSearch constraint
findings.caveat: Citation and holding not verified against a fetched primary source. Verify before it becomes load-bearing.

findings.claim: UK puts an explicit tax-free price on an employee's home electricity for work: HMRC allows a flat homeworking allowance with no tax or reporting
findings.number: GBP 6.00/week (GBP 26/month) from 2020-21 onwards; previously GBP 4.00/week (GBP 18/month) for 2012-13 to 2019-20
findings.source: GOV.UK, 'Expenses and benefits: homeworking — Homeworking expenses and benefits that are exempt from tax'
findings.caveat: Requires an agreed, regular homeworking arrangement. GBP 6/week is ~GBP 0.036/hr over a 168-hour week — same order as the energy cost, so the safe harbour would roughly cover a harvested machine.

findings.claim: Paying households for a controllable in-home resource is established large-scale utility practice — the closest operating precedent for Tier B compensation
findings.number: 10,658,027 US residential customers enrolled in demand response in 2024 (10,950,828 all sectors); 4,785 MW actual residential peak savings
findings.source: EIA Electric Power Annual, Table 10.3, 'Demand Response — Yearly Energy and Demand Savings', Form EIA-861

findings.claim: The going rate for that household precedent is low — a useful anchor for what consent costs
findings.number: $273.346M residential customer incentives 2024 over 10.658M households = ~$25.6/household-year (derived); $1.2247B all sectors
findings.source: EIA Electric Power Annual, Table 10.4, 'Demand Response — Program Costs', Form EIA-861; per-household figure derived against Table 10.3
findings.caveat: The per-household division is this analysis's arithmetic; EIA publishes only aggregate incentives and enrolment counts.

findings.claim: Organizations have already enrolled device fleets in donated distributed compute at scale — the operational template for Tier A and B exists
findings.number: 800,000+ people, 80 countries, 450 organizations, computing power of 7 million computers/phones/tablets; 6 billion+ calculations
findings.source: World Community Grid, About Us (worldcommunitygrid.org) — founded by IBM 2004, assets transferred to Krembil Research Institute (UHN) in 2021
findings.caveat: Cumulative lifetime totals, not concurrent devices; the page does not separate business-enrolled fleets from individual volunteers among the 450 organizations.

findings.claim: Intel/United Devices philanthropic 'screensaver' grids (2001-2007) are the other named corporate-fleet precedent
findings.number: ~3.5 million PCs claimed at peak
findings.source: Model knowledge; no primary source fetched (project sites defunct)
findings.caveat: Number not verified; treat as illustrative only.

findings.claim: Documented crypto-mining-on-employer-hardware incidents (the involuntary version of Tier B) exist but no primary record was retrievable here
findings.number: n/a
findings.source: Attempted NSF Office of Inspector General semiannual reports (nsf.gov/oig) — 404 on fetch
findings.caveat: Do not cite. The Harvard Odyssey Dogecoin incident (2014) and NSF OIG bitcoin-mining findings are recalled but unfetched.

at-home-tier-mechanics.notes:
TIER B VERDICT. (1) Operable: yes. Intune "runs entirely in the cloud, with no on-premises infrastructure required" and judges posture "not on whether the device is on the corporate network"; required endpoints are public FQDNs on TCP 443. Apple APNs needs only Ethernet/cellular/Wi-Fi to 17.0.0.0/8; DDM pushes enforcement into the device. A laptop at a kitchen table is as controllable as one at a desk. The binding constraint is consent, power billing and residential uplink, not technical reach.

(2) Whose cost: the employee's, ~31% premium (18.11 vs 13.79 c/kWh), moving harvest energy ~$0.003 to ~$0.004/hr. CA Labor Code 2802 makes indemnification mandatory. HMRC prices it at GBP 6/week tax-free, ~GBP 0.036/hr over a full week.

(3) Precedent: both ways. 10.66M US households in demand response, paid $273M/yr (~$26/household-year). World Community Grid: 450 organizations, 7M devices.

DURATION: 5.10 h of at-home work per work-at-home day, on 34.5% of workdays, so ~1.76 h/day and ~93% idle. More idle at home than at the office.

CAVEATS: ATUS is person-time, not device-on time. Cochran and the Intel figure UNVERIFIED; no mining incident retrieved. EIA 2025-26 preliminary.
